performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: The ninth piece in Mussorgsky’s Pictures at an Exhibition takes its subject from Hartmann’s design for a clock in the form of a hut on chicken legs; Mussorgsky portrayed its witch, Baba Yaga, flying through the air in a mortar. The movement leads without a break into The Great Gate of Kyiv.

sections.label: A · Allegro con brio, feroce, repeated Gs
sections.mNote: Feroce; hard accents and repeated Gs open the section.

sections.label: B · Andante mosso, flute above bass
sections.mNote: Rocking thirds surround the low tune in the Andante mosso.

sections.label: A′ · Allegro molto, repeated G returns
sections.mNote: Allegro molto brings back the opening two-beat figure.

sections.label: Coda · Rising octaves, Allegro molto
sections.mNote: Continuous semiquavers rise into the finale without a break.

cues.title: Opening, F♯ and low G
cues.text: F♯ and low G sound together, followed by a whole bar of silence. The Gs are soon repeated in hammered strokes. The marking is feroce (ferocious), and Ravel gives a trumpet theme against this, with other brass replying.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 1–56; trumpet and brass scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Andante mosso, flute and bass
cues.text: In the Andante mosso, a flute plays above a slower line in bassoon and double bass. The middle section opens with G and E alternating. Harp, celesta and strings accompany the low melody.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, Andante mosso, bars 95 onward; instruments: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hartmann’s design for a clock
cues.text: Hartmann’s sketch is a design for a metal clock in the form of a little hut on chicken legs, decorated with cocks’ heads. Mussorgsky added the hut’s owner, Baba Yaga, who flies about in a mortar hunting for victims.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg describes the clock and Baba Yaga’s mortar: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition. Peter Laki identifies the surviving sketch: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky

cues.title: Earlier witches’ sabbath, 1867
cues.text: Mussorgsky had already written a sabbath. Balakirev refused to perform his St John’s Night on the Bare Mountain, finished on St John’s Eve 1867. Orrin Howard of the LA Phil heard in Baba Yaga’s ride Mussorgsky’s “best Bald Mountain pictorialism”.
cues.evidence: Mussorgsky’s inscription on the score, finished on the eve of St John’s Day, 23 June 1867, and Balakirev’s refusal to perform it: https://www.belcanto.ru/mussorgsky_night.html (Russian). Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, p. 220: the piece, then called St. John’s Eve, was “severely and justly criticized by Balakireff”: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf . Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note on Pictures at an Exhibition: https://www.laphil.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-modest-mussorgsky-zs2phpn9

cues.title: Return of the opening, Allegro molto
cues.text: At the Allegro molto the repeated Gs return in two-beat bars. The trumpet’s strident tune comes back, and the brass reply to it.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 123 onward; orchestral return: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing run and attacca
cues.text: The closing semiquavers run up through octave after octave to G. The movement is marked attacca, and the G leads without a pause into the E♭ major opening of The Great Gate of Kyiv.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, Baba Yaga bars 187–211 and the first bar of The Great Gate: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/baba-allegro-molto.ily
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repeated G becomes rocking G–E figure
transitions.from: A · Allegro con brio, feroce, repeated Gs
transitions.to: B · Andante mosso, flute above bass
transitions.how: The hard repeated Gs reduce to a quiet figure rocking between G and E, and Andante mosso slows the pulse. Ravel brings flute, bassoon and double bass forward, with harp and celesta around them, and withdraws the heavy brass.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 89–103: repeated G, Andante mosso and rocking G–E figure. Scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: From the tremolo to Allegro molto
transitions.from: B · Andante mosso, flute above bass
transitions.to: A′ · Allegro molto, repeated G returns
transitions.how: The middle section ends with a tremolo on B, D♯ and G held under a fermata. A forceful G begins the Allegro molto, and the bars return to two beats. The repeated-note figure comes back, followed by the brass tune. In Lamm’s piano edition the passage runs from bar 122 to bar 145.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 122–145: final tremolo, fermata and G-led Allegro molto; the orchestral return is described by Joanna Wyld.

transitions.title: Semiquaver octaves lead into E♭ major
transitions.from: A′ · Allegro molto, repeated G returns
transitions.how: The short phrases turn into continuous semiquavers in octaves. These run downwards, then climb to G, the third of the E♭ major chord that opens the finale. The last bar is marked attacca, and The Great Gate follows without a break.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 187–211 and the opening of The Great Gate; Mutopia transcription. Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note also describes the uninterrupted join.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
